title: Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hundreds of protesters blocked the parade route after it was given clearance for the first time in almost 30 years
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hundreds of protesters blocked the parade route after it was given clearance for the first time in almost 30 yearsByCommunity correspondent, BBC News NIHistory shows that when the politics of Northern Ireland are wrapped up in a street dispute, friction is seldom far away.Bitter rows in the Stormont chamber between unionists and nationalists happen almost every week, but ground-level arguments are rare these days.The Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown is a clash of political cultures.The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation. The area where it wants to walk is largely Catholic, and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.This dispute over a piece of road is not just a local problem. It has the potential to affect other parts of Northern Ireland and the power-sharing arrangements at Stormont."What happens at Drumcree never stays at Drumcree," was how one retired politician put it.When the parade dispute first erupted into violence in the mid-1990s, the disorder spread to other places - and almost derailed the peace process.But while it was never fully resolved, the dispute faded over the next 30 years. Its sudden re-emergence has caught most people by surprise, including many politicians.What happened was that a legal case was brought to court over the dispute early this summer, re-opening the debate.The two largest parties in Northern Ireland, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), have been on opposite sides of the argument.Sinn Féin are firmly behind the residents. The DUP fully supports the Orange Order.They may be partners in the devolved government at Stormont, but when it comes to Drumcree they could not be further apart.As always in Northern Ireland, the historical context is important.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Orangemen waited in the Drumcree church hall for the go-ahead to proceed down the Garvaghy RoadAlthough there has been an uneasy calm in Portadown over the parading issue in recent years, the Orange Order regards the march as unfinished business.In 1998, it was banned from completing its Drumcree march - which includes the Garvaghy Road - and has been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route ever since.It has applied and been turned down more than 1,000 times in the past three decades.It says it is being denied a traditional walk which dates back to the early 1800s.A Parades Commission was set up in the late 1990s to adjudicate on marching disputes and, until now, it has consistently ruled against the route.The Orange Order's legal challenge to a ruling in June this year succeeded on procedural grounds.The order subsequently re-applied for permission to carry out the parade, albeit a scaled-back version with only 35 participants rather than 400 - and was successful.Nationalist residents on the Garvaghy Road were left shocked and angry.For them, the parade is triumphalist and unwelcome in the area.Rather than being about tradition, they see the parade as an act of supremacy and say it re-opens old community wounds.During a last-minute legal battle over the march, a judge appealed for all sides of the dispute to find common ground and come to an agreement.Nobody was surprised when that did not happen.Feelings are running high on the issue on all sides, including among the political parties.Relations in the power-sharing executive are now dangerously close to breaking point.There is a Stormont election next year which means parties tend to dig in, rather than search for compromises.The Drumcree dispute goes to the heart of the divisions which remain in Northern Ireland.Events of recent days are a reminder that the peace process is not over, it is ongoing - and there is still work to be done on the ground and at Stormont.

schema.headline: Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland

title: What we know about RAF Fairford incident and counter-terror probe
description: Image caption, Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded areaByEmily AtkinsonUpdated 2 hours
body: Image caption, Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded areaByEmily AtkinsonUpdated 2 hours agoFive men have been arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences after a major incident was declared at an airbase in the west of England.Bomb disposal teams have been examining a number of vehicles near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire and dozens of homes in the surrounding area have been evacuated.Here is a summary of what we know so far.Where is RAF Fairford?RAF Fairford is located in the Cotswolds, about four miles (6.4km) south of the town of Fairford, which sits along the River Coln.The base shares a long history with the American military, and has recently been used by US warplanes as a staging post for defensive strikes on Iran.What happened?Gloucestershire Police said they received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on Sunday.Five men were later arrested by its officers near Whelford, a village around two miles (3.2km) south-east of the base.A bomb disposal team was also deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles, police said, around which a 400m (1,312ft) cordon is in place.Aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching two stationary white vans in a wooded area, though its use has not been confirmed by police.Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) is leading the investigation into the incident. The BBC understands the operation was not intelligence led.The US military said it was "working closely" with its UK counterparts "to monitor this situation, minimise impacts and ensure the safety of US personnel, their families, and the local community".There has been a large emergency service presence in the area since the early hours of Sunday, which Gloucestershire Police Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth said would remain over the next few days.Blyth told a news conference on Sunday evening that the force would continue to assist CTP and liaise with other national partners.She also said she would leave any declaration of a "terrorist incident" to CTP.Figure caption, Watch: What we know about the counter-terrorism operation near RAF FairfordWho are the suspects?Five men were initially detained on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act.They were then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.The men, who remain in custody, have not been named. Police have not said where they are being held.Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests without an extension application.Asked whether police were seeking other individuals in connection with the incident, Blyth said she believed the matter was "contained".US President Donald Trump said those arrested were "looking to do big damage", adding: "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them."Image caption, This image has been circulating following the arrests of five men near RAF FairfordBBC Your Voice has received an image purporting to show the moment five men were arrested.It showed detained men in Whelford, about 350m (1,148ft) from runway access at Crash Gate 6A at RAF Fairford.The BBC has been unable to verify the original source but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic.How many homes have been evacuated?Gloucestershire Police said displaced residents have been told they will not be able to return to their homes on Sunday night.Overnight accommodation will be found by Cotswold District Council for those affected who are unable to stay with family and friends, according to Deputy Chief Executive David Stanley.Eighty-five households were evacuated following the incident and urged to shelter at a nearby leisure centre.Several people have told the BBC they were woken by police in the early hours of Sunday and ordered to leave."We just had to throw our clothes on and come. We didn't know anything," one resident, who named herself only as Jo, said.Another resident, Jason, said: "It all happened very quickly. We just packed our stuff up and came here."Several people in the leisure centre are still wearing their pyjamas, according to a BBC reporter there.What have eyewitnesses said?A local resident told the BBC she alerted the police to suspicious activity near the base early on Sunday.The woman, who did not want to be named, said she initially called the Ministry of Defence (MoD) police but nobody answered, and then called 999. She said she had seen three parked vans and a group of men wearing masks.The MoD declined to comment.Another resident described the moment he said he saw police apprehend the suspects.Jeff told the BBC he heard "shouting outside his front door", although he could not be sure where it came from.He said he then looked out of his window and saw "people being held by police outside".Figure caption, Watch: Police told us to leave our home immediately, says local residentWhat has the UK government said?Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "deeply concerning" and the government would "always take every step necessary" to protect people.His defence secretary, Wes Streeting, declined to comment on a live operation but said he had been in contact with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth.Asked at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool whether there was any Iranian involvement, he said it was "far too early to comment or speculate, and it would be irresponsible for me to do so".What is RAF Fairford used for?RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.The base was occupied by USAF Strategic Air Command during the Cold War and later the first Gulf War in 1991.B-52 bombers were also deployed by USAF from RAF Fairford on raids to Iraq in 2003.It was most recently used on 1 March, following a decision by former UK prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to allow the US to use UK bases - including RAF Fairford - for "defensive" strikes on Iranian capabilities.Conflict was sparked across the Middle East after the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February.Iran responded by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf.

schema.headline: What we know about RAF Fairford incident and counter-terror probe

title: Nations League: Craig Bellamy 'hurting' as Wales outclassed by Denmark
description: Defeat - which came just three days after a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon - has left Wales with plenty of work to do.They will at least have home adv
body: Defeat - which came just three days after a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon - has left Wales with plenty of work to do.They will at least have home advantage at Cardiff City Stadium as they prepare for the remainder of the current international break, with matches against Norway on Thursday, 1 October, and then Denmark the following Sunday.Captain Davies felt Wales were being taught some harsh lessons in what is their second stint in the top tier of the Nations League."It was a tough game. They are a good team and made it a hard game for us," the Spurs defender told BBC Match of the Day Wales."It was really frustrating to concede from two set-pieces. The Nations League games are against the best teams in Europe, it was always going to be tough."If you're not at 100% then you are going to get punished at this level. We have to regroup and go again on Thursday."Despite the setback in the Danish capital, winger Sorba Thomas echoed Bellamy's sentiments."Thankfully we've got two games at home still to come. We'll have home advantage so we need to show a reaction," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales."We are just going to get better. We are a small nation but we've got big hearts and beliefs and for us it's about showing that more on the pitch."

schema.headline: Nations League: Craig Bellamy 'hurting' as Wales outclassed by Denmark

title: Chelsea: Resilience is back so can Blues regain the WSL title this season?
description: Sonia Bompastor led Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in her first season in charge, but it did not go to plan in 2025-26 as their six-year stran
body: Sonia Bompastor led Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in her first season in charge, but it did not go to plan in 2025-26 as their six-year stranglehold on the WSL ended.City overtook them at the top and many believed Arsenal would be the main challengers this season after a strong summer's recruitment.Perhaps written off, Chelsea started the season tamely, drawing 1-1 with Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite a dominant performance.The same issues were rife as they lacked ruthlessness in front of goal and a mistake at the back gifted Villa an opportunity. But since then, Chelsea have turned dominant performances into results, winning three matches in a row, capping it off with a well-rounded display against Arsenal, who are seven points behind City in seventh spot.Bompastor said her side were prepared to "mentally fight" and able to "adjust" to Arsenal's pressure in a way perhaps they didn't last season. It was a defensive masterclass and they delivered Bompastor's gameplan perfectly, capping off victory with a third successive clean sheet - a run of 315 minutes without conceding a goal."In this league, you have so many different opponents and you have to be able to adjust and do something different," said the Blues boss. "I've been talking a lot about that, to be strong and to be together, I always want to see a group of players who are together in those high and low moments. "We came into this game well prepared. We knew we would have moments in the game where we were not in control. We prepared for those moments. "We knew exactly where we wanted them to take the ball and where to leave some spaces. We were really strong mentally and physically."It is a result that could be the catalyst Chelsea needed to push on and put pressure on Manchester City, who face Arsenal next in the WSL (Sunday, 16:30 BST).Chelsea's match-winner Alyssa Thompson said their victory over the Gunners was "amazing for team morale".Even Bompastor admitted Chelsea are "a different team from last season" and there are tangible examples of their improvements.England midfielder Keira Walsh was a standout performer against Arsenal and it was her strike which was parried into the path of Thompson for the only goal.Her new parternship with 20-year-old Lexi Potter is flourishing and has allowed Walsh to get further up the pitch and play with more freedom.Bompastor said the 29-year-old was "a boss on the pitch" when she reaches those levels and it helps the team have "better foundations".Goalscorer Thompson has consistently delivered up front, while the arrival of summer signing Melvine Malard from Manchester United has given them an outlet.The French striker missed their opening two matches with a minor injury but scored on her debut against Birmingham City and caused havoc against Arsenal."She's massive for us. She puts in work off the ball and sets off the press," said team-mate Walsh. "Her awareness of people around her and her ability... She's an incredible striker and she will be very good for us."That press, led by Malard, has moved higher up and teams have struggled to break through, while full-back Ellie Carpenter continues to overlap dangerously.Katie McCabe, who switched from Arsenal to Chelsea this summer, has brought leadership and bite - an aggression that was lacking at times last season.Most of all, the Blues look like a team who believe they should be champions and are willing to work for it.It was in contrast to toothless Arsenal, who have one victory in their first four WSL games and scored just twice."We've got both sides to our game and we showed that tonight in spells. Everyone was fighting for each other. Every first and second ball was ours," added Walsh.

schema.headline: Chelsea: Resilience is back so can Blues regain the WSL title this season?

title: Thousands of Sussex homes affected and roads flooded after burst pipe
description: Thousands of homes in parts of West Sussex have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "signific
body: Thousands of homes in parts of West Sussex have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak.Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said. Southern Water said about 9,000 customers were impacted, but as of 19:45 BST, most customers had seen their supplies restored.A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies."The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green. It first reported at 12:00 that supplies had returned to some homes. Southern Water said its teams were still carrying out repairs but the damaged section of pipe had been removed and its replacement installed."We apologise for this disruption and would like to thank customers for their patience while we complete the repair," it added.John Boulton, who is 82, and his partner were without water earlier. He said: "It's pretty disgusting, really - we pay so much for the water supply."Boulton said he had just paid £22 for bottled water in a shop.

schema.headline: Thousands of Sussex homes affected and roads flooded after burst pipe

title: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up."The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home."People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recentlyIn Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times"."Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore."But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air."The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lecturesBorn in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects   Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home."When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity."If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

schema.headline: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton sets up huge win in series decider
description: Third Metro Bank one-day international, Kia Oval England 355-7 (50 overs): Banton 126, Brook 77, Cox 76Sri Lanka 132 (29.1 overs): Kusal 35; Dawson 3-
body: Third Metro Bank one-day international, Kia Oval England 355-7 (50 overs): Banton 126, Brook 77, Cox 76Sri Lanka 132 (29.1 overs): Kusal 35; Dawson 3-26England won by 223 runsScorecardTom Banton delivered on all of his potential by crashing a brilliant first international century as England wrapped up their summer with an ODI series win over Sri Lanka.The 27-year-old right-hander was once the rising star of English cricket when handed a debut in 2019 but afterwards fell out of love with the game after losing his way.After reaching his hundred in 95 balls in the third one-day international at The Oval, he stood with arms wide and looked to the sky - all of that disappointment seemingly behind him. "My fiance, Lilly, was here and all of her family," Banton said."Unfortunately, my mum, dad and brother weren't here because whenever my mum seems to come I don't do that well."Bless her, she is not banned from coming, but she avoids coming now."The opener went on to make 126 from 105 deliveries, perfectly countering tricky early conditions - conditions in which Joe Root struggled uncharacteristically for 18 from 37 balls - and going on to share an increasingly aggressive stand of 150 in 117 balls with captain Harry Brook."To score a hundred for England is just the best feeling on earth," Banton said. "I don't think anything is going to beat it."Brook made 77 and Jordan Cox, picked in the place of the injured Jos Buttler, added a 52-ball 76 to lift England to 355-7.That always appeared a match-winning total on a surface offering bounce for the pace bowlers and turn for the spinners.Sri Lanka crumbled to 132 all out in 29.1 overs, giving England a 223-run win and their biggest ODI victory against the tourists. It meant England signed off their summer, one that included off-field issues, the end of Bazball, Ben Stokes' retirement and Root's surprise return as Test skipper, with a fifth successive series win amid the madness across formats.Banton's success is heartwarming. When, fresh out of Second XI cricket, he made his debut as a 20-year-old in 2019 he was seen as England's next big thing.He was in the same England Under-19 team as Brook but, rather than the Yorkshireman who is now captain, it was the Somerset product who was given the opportunity when Eoin Morgan's World Cup-winning side needed a fresh face on its journey forward.Tougher times followed, resulting in almost five years out of the 50-over side and only occasional T20 appearances.During that time Kevin Pietersen, now an England mentor, said Banton "has all the talent but, at the moment, he is wasting it".It was comparisons to Pietersen which Banton struggled with. Last week, Banton said remains "in awe" of the iconic England batter.With thrilling reverse sweeps here, he showed the invention that drew those comparisons. He was also vicious on the pull, hit classically through the covers and, when Ben Duckett was bowled in the second over and Root faced 13 dot balls in a row, did not panic.By the time he was dismissed he had hit 16 fours and five sixes.When he walked off he turned and raised his bat amid a standing ovation from The Oval crowd – as Pietersen famously did 21 years ago.Banton only has the opportunity as opener here because of Jacob Bethell's injury.He may find himself out of the XI when England begin a tri-series in Pakistan - a series that also involves Sri Lanka - on 20 October.The tourists, impressive in setting up this decider on Thursday, were poor here. They had already dropped Root before he was dismissed and wicketkeeper and captain Kusal Mendis spilled a thick edge when Brook had seven.Afterwards the England captain started slowly but he kicked it into life from a position of 108-2 after 25 overs.Also encouraging was the performance of Cox, whose knock also built on a slow start and followed an impressive run in the Test side against Pakistan.Sonny Baker, recalled for his second ODI in place of Josh Tongue, nicked off Pathum Nissanka with a quick, swinging and rising delivery two balls into the second over, after which Sri Lanka did not recover. Left-arm spinner Liam Dawson also repaid the faith for his inclusion over Rehan Ahmed with figures of 3-26.This summer has provided so many issues for England, including the end of Brendon McCullum's reign as Test coach.Still his ODI side now has momentum - a third series win a row - as it builds towards next year's World Cup. Series in Pakistan, Australia and South Africa are to come this winter.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton sets up huge win in series decider

title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
description: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspon
body: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondentReporting fromTaiz, Yemen"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire."Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goatsHe told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach."We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weaponsTaiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line."It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.Image source, Liam Weir/BBC NewsImage caption, Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goatsIn the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this monthAbout 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day."We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain."We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclistFatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said."I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

schema.headline: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control

title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
description: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption,
body: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date ByStephanie HegartyBBC World Service correspondentAshlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.Pike told Sellars she did not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when Colleen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murderBut Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, while UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider."It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence."Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parentsIn 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later, it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged over a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.In 2021, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her."Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say'She should pay for it'Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment and Lee has never before granted clemency in a death penalty case.The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution."She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via ReutersImage caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added."There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it was what Colleen's family want."We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption."When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says."These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime."People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says."Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

schema.headline: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row

title: Nepal: Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
description: Rescuers have recovered two bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas.Around a d
body: Rescuers have recovered two bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas.Around a dozen people are still thought to be missing after a sheet of snow fell on the base camp of Himlung Himal peak on Manang district on Sunday morning.The group of Nepalese nationals, including climbers and support staff, had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp and fix ropes.Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams initially unable to reach the site.Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP that at least eight members of his expedition team had been reported missing. The exact number of climbers still unaccounted for remains unclear.A rescue team consisting of experienced mountaineers was rushed from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, via helicopter. That effort is now expected to continue on Monday due to the thick snow and bad weather, local media report.The Nepalese team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.The latest death of Nepalese climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja.It also comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.Extreme weather events have also affected other parts of Asia in the past week.Extreme weather in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.Meanwhile, a flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok because of heavy rainfall since Thursday, with people being urged to stay at home or move to higher floors.Earlier this week, a deadly typhoon that battered Tokyo, triggering landslides in neighbouring prefectures that killed four people.Typhoon Dujuan was the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", an area of warmer sea water that facilitates the formation of powerful storms.

schema.headline: Nepal: Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp

title: Andy Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
description: Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general elect
body: Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month.While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded. Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work."There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded.When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high."He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out".Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there".Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS."He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus".Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer.On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament."The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide."Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them.He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget."Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care.He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy."He told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms.The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Burnham can show he is "serious about fixing care" by getting on with the cross-party talks that began in July.He added: "This can't just be a series of No 10 headlines with no real action."Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax."He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead."Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy.He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government.It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died.The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election.At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000.The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England

title: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey
description: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 27 September 2026 13:34 BSTTens of millions
body: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 27 September 2026 13:34 BSTTens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree.Figure caption, BBC Weather presenter Helen Willetts look at the impacts of the powerful Nor'easterThe nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware.A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities floodedNWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines."Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhoodA professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New JerseyImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts

schema.headline: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey

title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit
description: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vi
body: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context."It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement."It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church"."How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain.

schema.headline: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit

title: Police granted more time to quiz Manchester plot suspects
description: The two men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, the force said on Tuesday.Sources told the BBC that the
body: The two men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, the force said on Tuesday.Sources told the BBC that the suspected plot was "fairly imminent" and in the later stages of planning.Police said searches at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford had also taken place.Yom Kippur is considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.A spokesperson for the Community Security Trust, which coordinates security for Jewish communities in the UK, said on Tuesday that the suspected plot was "utterly chilling coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year".They added: "[This] is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time."

schema.headline: Police granted more time to quiz Manchester plot suspects
